Researchers have been developing self-sensing composite materials that can detect and locate damage within the material using embedded piezoelectric sensors. These sensors use an active method, specifically an iterative inversion of a discrete-time system, to identify and correct for damage. However, this method has limitations in accuracy due to the complex, non-linear nature of damage. To address this issue, a new approach has been proposed that combines a Gaussian Process model with the active method, utilizing genetic algorithms to optimize the model's parameters for damage detection accuracy. This approach has been tested on a composite beam with simulated damage, and the results have shown that the proposed method can significantly improve the accuracy of damage reconstruction compared to the traditional active method.

A novel framework is proposed to integrate various forms of intelligence into the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model. This model demonstrates how different levels of rationality in both predators and preys can be simulated by adjusting the variables of production and consumption rates. By applying a co-existence condition, we can determine when the populations will either thrive or decline based on their respective forms of rationality. Our analysis reveals that when predators and preys operate under full rationality, there is a co-existence region where the populations will persist, bounded by areas of extinction when either group acts purely instinctively. Our findings can be visually represented using a 3D graph, and they have potential applications in understanding and managing real-world ecosystems, as well as financial markets.

A new approach based on geometric vectors is proposed to establish integral identities, building on the work of Gou and Ma (2019). This approach allows for the proof of a broad class of identities, including those previously demonstrated by Gou and Ma (2020).

To explore the potential of the muon g-2 anomaly and enhance the sensitivity to new physics beyond the Standard Model, we suggest implementing a muonium-to-muon conversion process within a muon storage ring, specifically within the Fermilab muon g-2 experimental setup. To effectively search for this conversion process, we recommend constructing a compact, high-intensity muonium beam and measuring the resulting muon decay electrons. With an optimal beam intensity of 10^13 muonium pulses per second, the expected limit on the conversion probability would reach 10^-12, potentially narrowing the region beyond the current experimental area by a factor of ten.

We establish the spin-three Ward identities within the Toda conformal field theory, showing they align with the Toda version of higher-spin symmetry, and derive the corresponding equations of motion for the Toda fields, which match known results.

We establish that all uniform lattices within the class of p-adic analytic groups possess the property of being biautomatic. This achievement is made possible by the development of specific patching rules for automatic groups, in response to a notion of group presentations with parameters.

Neurological disorders like spinal cord injuries and stroke can severely limit a person's ability to walk, impacting their independence and quality of life. To restore walking abilities, it is crucial to accurately predict the complex muscle activation patterns that occur during gait using brain signals. This study compares two methods of recording brain activity, EEG and ECoG, in order to develop a model that can effectively forecast walking-related muscle activation. By analyzing the results, we found that the ECoG-based model outperformed the EEG-based one in terms of prediction accuracy, with the former achieving a higher correlation between predicted and actual muscle activation patterns. This study provides valuable insights into the potential of using brain signals to control prosthetic limbs and other assistive devices, and highlights the importance of continued research in this area.

We demonstrate that for a right-angled Artin group $A(\Gamma)$, if a subgraph $\gamma$ of its defining graph $\Gamma$ is disconnected in a way that isolates a component from the rest, the group can act on a specific type of tree with an isomorphic subgroup at isolated vertices' stabilizers and an interconnected component's stabilizers forming an isomorphic group within the vertex stabilizers of a larger, related tree. This action's isomorphism properties depend on whether the isolated or interconnected components of $\gamma$'s defining graph isomorphism classes.

Dynamic time-varying graphs exhibit a complex structure with multiple dimensions, posing significant challenges for dynamic node classification tasks. Traditional methods typically focus on a single dimension of evolution, neglecting the interplay between various node features and temporal dynamics. To address this limitation, we propose DECENNT, a multi-dimensional evolution learning framework for dynamic node classification that captures diverse dimensions of graph dynamics through independent attention mechanisms. DECENNT assigns a dedicated memory bank to each dimension, enabling the model to store and update node representations for that dimension. Through an attention mechanism, DECENNT dynamically combines these representations to form the final node representation, adaptively selecting the most relevant dimension(s) based on the current graph structure. DECENNT's design allows for efficient model training and inference, even in large-scale time-varying graphs with missing data. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate DECENNT's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art dynamic node classification models.

Distinguishing between biological and non-biological objects in motion is a challenging task. To address this issue, we propose a novel method called BioMotion, which utilizes a generative adversarial network to synthesize motion trajectories of biological objects. This approach enables the discrimination of biological and non-biological objects in video streams through a subsequent binary classifier. BioMotion leverages the discriminative power of the GAN to differentiate between biological and non-biological motion in the latent space, which can be trained with a minimal dataset. Our approach demonstrates significant improvements in distinguishing biological and non-biological objects in the video stream, with an 11.4% increase in F1-score compared to using a standard classifier trained on bounding box trajectories.

We introduce a new method, known as the Nested Neumann algorithm, to solve the Neumann problem for low-incline convex shapes in two dimensions. Our solution leverages an exact solution to an adjacent Neumann problem to develop a finite, non-rectangular grid, which then allows the original issue to be solved. We assess the effectiveness of our method using numerical tests on various convex shapes, including polygons and smooth curves, and compare our results to alternative methods. Our findings show that the Nested Neumann algorithm converges rapidly, particularly for shapes with small initial mass excess, and that its convergence rate can be influenced by factors such as the number of neumann nodes and the concept of inception depth.

Through the application of the winding number, we have developed an approach to identify and analyze the topological properties of an Anderson insulator within a two-dimensional lattice that exhibits long-range interactions and disorder. By employing the spectral function, we have successfully determined the winding number solely based on current measurements in a system that is topologically trivial and one that is topologically nontrivial. Furthermore, we have established the relationship between the winding number and the conductance in both single-channel and multi-channel scenarios. In order to validate our theoretical findings, we have utilized the tight-binding model to investigate the behavior of an Anderson lattice that is randomly occupied and one that is fully occupied, and we have observed the universal scaling behavior of the winding number and the fractional quantum Hall effect in the Anderson insulator.

We propose that the invariants derived from genus-one curves embody independent geometric characteristics, reflecting a common underlying structure through their various computations. Our approach leverages the curve's embedding within the Jacobian variety of the genus-one system and its associated divisor, allowing us to derive a set of invariants via the law of conservation of number applied to the Jacobian variety. These invariants form the basis for a new, distinct set of values computed using the genus-one system's modular parametrization and the associated Hecke operators. The relationship between the two sets of invariants is explored and compared to other comparable studies.

To produce heavy Higgs bosons through bottom squark pair annihilation in the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, precise calculations of the cross section are necessary, taking into account complex parameters and their phases. A comprehensive formula has been developed to calculate the cross section for heavy Higgs boson pair production, accounting for the phases of complex parameters and the impact of top and bottom squark contributions. Furthermore, a detailed analysis has been conducted to determine the regions of complex parameter phases where the squark impact is most pronounced, particularly in the context of the Large Hadron Collider.

In the contextual linear bandit problem, an agent learns to choose actions based on input data and receives feedback in the form of a scalar value. This paper addresses a specific scenario where the input data is part of an infinite-dimensional context that is either known to the learner or must be communicated through communication channels. The goal is to minimize regret, which is influenced by the smoothness of the underlying linear function and the level of noise present in the data. The author demonstrates that when the context is known, regret can be achieved with a specific level of precision, and when the context is unknown, it can be learned through communication channels with a level of precision that is directly related to the noise present. Additionally, the paper shows that these results are difficult to improve upon. The results are then applied to a contextual linear bandit problem with a Gaussian prior, demonstrating that the regret can be achieved with a specific level of precision.

Recent efficient methods for estimating policy values in new environments rely on comparing the new setting to similar past experiences. These approaches apply universally but require substantial computational resources to calculate values in unfamiliar settings. This study introduces two techniques to reduce the computational burden of applying efficient value function estimators while maintaining high-accuracy estimates of policy values. The first method is specifically designed to improve the performance in large-scale settings by utilizing a simplified representation of the policy and its associated value function. The second method, in contrast, is applicable to all settings and involves selecting a random subset of states to calculate values for, rather than for every possible state. The impact of varying testing sample sizes on the performance of these efficient value function estimates was also investigated. The results obtained in this study are both theoretical and empirical, with applications to both discrete and continuous policy settings.

In 2017, measurements of charged hadron, specifically pions, kaons, and protons, transverse momentum distributions in relation to their first harmonic flow in Au+Au mid-central collisions at a 7.7 GeV/nucleon energy were conducted. These findings were compared to theoretical calculations using the EPOS LHC and V.0.2rC hydrodynamic models. The data aligned closely with V.0.2rC predictions for both pions and protons, whereas kaon and pion to proton yield ratios showed some discrepancies with the model. The transverse momentum ranges where pions and protons behave like thermal particles were found to be significantly wider than expected from their rest masses, indicating the presence of additional nonthermal mechanisms.

In complex networks with high levels of interference, binary power control is shown through performance analysis to nearly match the efficiency of optimal power control. Key performance metrics, including the set of parameters for which binary power control is feasible and the maximum achievable data rates, are examined for both optimal and binary power control. The study's findings are validated using a real-world scenario with access points and mobile devices.

A new method called multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA) has been developed to enhance the computational efficiency of simulating flows with suspended particles. This algorithm takes advantage of the fact that particles move at a slower speed than the fluid around them, allowing for the use of larger time steps for calculating particle motion while maintaining a smaller time step for fluid flow. An adaptive strategy has been implemented to dynamically adjust the time steps for particles and fluid, ensuring second-order accuracy and satisfying constraints imposed by the immersed boundary method. Tests have demonstrated that the TAJIK flow past a square at a Reynolds number of 100 can be accurately simulated, and the algorithm achieves a computational cost that scales linearly with the desired accuracy. Compared to a standard time-step approach, the algorithm achieves a significant reduction in computational cost, achieving a $\Delta t^2$ scaling over a wide range of time step sizes.

For two positive integers a and b, the equation $7^p=a^2+b^3$ has been solved to determine its solutions. Additionally, for another prime number q where q is not equal to 1 mod 9, the equation $7^n=a^2+b^q$ has been extended to have a finite number of solutions.

This paper introduces a novel approach for a single-legged hopping robot to navigate complex terrain by employing a tail for stability. The approach uses feedback control to accurately follow a planned hopping sequence and accounts for the tail's impact on the hopping dynamics. By analyzing the relationship between the tail's movement and the forces it generates, feedback control is applied to counteract forces in specific directions. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through simulations of a hopping robot with a tail on soft ground, showing its ability to follow planned trajectories and recover from disturbances.

A novel method has been developed to determine the charge radii of mesons using an improved vector and tensor meson charge radii calculation technique. This approach employs the world-conformal gauge in a theory that incorporates two colors and three flavors, with meson charge radii values obtained through current correlation functions and verified against values derived from energy spectrum and wave function. The charge radii values are found to scale linearly with distance, which in turn scales with the color-kinetic term coefficient $\sqrt{\kappa|\Lambda|}$. The calculated tensor meson charge radii values show a decline as the distance increases, in contrast to the linear scaling exhibited by vector meson charge radii values.

A significant amount of information on the internet is organized into document networks, where web pages, news articles, and social media posts are interconnected based on references, shared links, or reposts. These connections can provide valuable insights into the relationships between documents and the underlying topics they discuss. We introduce a novel HDTM that leverages document networks to uncover semantic relationships and discover common topics. By analyzing the links between documents, we can identify initial topic connections, refine them, and discover underlying document attributes. The HDTM employs a hierarchical approach to model relationships at different levels, enabling it to capture both common and unique topics. We assess the model's effectiveness in various applications, including identifying document outliers, classifying documents, and discovering document attributes. The results show that the HDTM outperforms traditional statistical techniques and current HDTM approaches in analyzing networked documents and revealing the topics they discuss.

Quantum annealing is a computational approach that leverages the natural behavior of a quantum system to find its lowest energy state, which corresponds to a problem's optimal solution. To achieve this, it's essential to understand how to time the annealing process effectively. This study investigates the ideal annealing gap for the Motzkin string problem, which is crucial for determining the ideal annealing duration. A gap-finding method is developed and applied to identify the ideal gap and its associated times. Furthermore, a way is proposed to determine the ideal annealing gap without prior knowledge, which is essential for determining the ideal annealing duration.

To investigate the magnetic and superconducting properties of nickelates, we employed a local self-consistent Gaussian approximation method to calculate the exchange parameters of an effective spin model. By analyzing the band structures of infinite-layer and 111-phase nickelates, we determined the parameters' symmetries and estimated their values. Notably, the exchange parameters of infinite-layer nickelates exhibit greater on-site Coulomb repulsion and a higher density of d-orbitals near the Fermi level compared to cuprates, making them highly promising for exploring unconventional superconductivity.

This paper investigates the impact of a deconfinement phase transition on the equation of state and the formation of quark stars within the context of two-flavor quantum chromodynamics. It is demonstrated that a smooth crossover phase transition can be treated as a continuous transition from non-relativistic to relativistic quarks, which can be effectively modeled using a simple modification of the mass term in the Lagrangian. By utilizing a perturbative approach, it is possible to derive the pressure of relativistic quarks in terms of the strong coupling constant, which can be matched to the quark mass model to obtain the equation of state. It is further shown that this equation of state can be matched to the observed properties of quark stars.

Quantum compass states, which are superpositions of classical states, are expected to be highly sensitive to small damping values, making them suitable for precise measurements. This study investigates how quantum compass states interact with a small environment, specifically a two-level system experiencing weak coupling with a power-law bath. We examine how these states respond to damping and calculate their number variance, a key indicator of their sensitivity to small damping parameters. We also determine the optimal initial classical configurations that minimize number variance, which in turn can be used for accurate damping parameter estimation. Notably, we found that certain positions of these configurations are immune to damping and can serve as reliable references in measurement experiments. We discuss how these findings can be applied to enhance the precision of damping parameter estimation and propose a method for estimating these parameters with high precision.

A new radiative transfer model, called R2, has been developed to accurately simulate the thermal balance of protoplanetary disks, particularly in their outer regions where cooling is heavily influenced by dust. Unlike previous models, R2 incorporates the impact of a specific type of radiation on the short-wavelength thermal balance of the disk, which is crucial in its far reaches. By including this factor, R2 reveals that the outer regions of disks are cooler and emit less heat than previously thought, with temperatures and emitted heat declining significantly beyond 100 astronomical units. These findings have important implications for the formation of giant planets through gravitational instability, as well as for interpreting observations of distant, warm planet candidates.

This study focuses on harmonic functions within the framework of gradient shrinking Ricci solitons, specifically investigating the relationship between the dimensionality of such functions and the curvature of the underlying manifold. We prove that if the harmonic function's growth rate is limited by a specific quadratic function of time, the dimensionality of the function is either zero or an integer greater than one, given sufficiently small curvature conditions. As a direct consequence, we establish that any 1-harmonic function under these conditions must be a constant value. We also extend these findings to include harmonic functions defined on harmonic-Hessian Einstein Ricci solitons.

Many recent static and dynamic backdoor attack methods have achieved high accuracy while maintaining the model's normal performance. However, they are difficult to deploy in various classification tasks due to the need to update the input file with clean samples. This paper introduces a novel trigger, the Dynamic Sequential Trigger (DST), which eliminates the requirement for inputting clean data by using a model modification method that only requires the initial delivery of the tampered model. The DST generates a series of different trigger forms through randomization, and the activation of each trigger is determined by an external input, the model input, or both. The DST can be activated based on the time, the model input, and other conditions, and it can be implemented with a minimal number of additional parameters. Experimental results on various datasets and neural network structures demonstrate the DST's effectiveness, robustness, and difficulty in detection.

Recent high-precision astrometric data from Gaia, collected over two years, reveals variations in the apparent movement of distant stars, particularly those located beyond the solar system. When analyzing these measurements in three-dimensional space, researchers found that the magnitude of movement changes significantly based on a star's position relative to the ecliptic plane, with stars at higher latitudes displaying much smaller shifts. To account for this phenomenon, when calculating parallax, the influence of the observer's motion around the Sun must be considered, primarily through Earth's orbital movement. This results in a characteristic shift in a star's apparent position, known as parallax, with its size determined by a star's actual distance and its movement across the sky influenced by the Earth's orbit. Ultimately, these measurements allow for the determination of genuine interstellar distances.

Our analysis of open question answering systems reveals their current limitations in handling factually incorrect answers, which can be misleading. To address this issue, we propose a method that utilizes a knowledge graph to answer questions and incorporates external knowledge, specifically from Wikipedia. This approach allows us to identify when answers are incorrect and incorporate the correct information. We tested this method using a correction dataset and found that it can accurately correct incorrect answers and incorporate correct incorrect information. Furthermore, we found that this approach is more effective at incorporating knowledge than traditional methods.

Recent, highly accurate measurements of the dipole moment for the (1,1) vibrational state of $CH^+$ have made it easier to create comprehensive spectral models for this small, oxygen-free molecular cation, which is crucial for understanding the composition of the lower ionosphere on Mars and Venus. However, creating spectral models for small molecular cations containing oxygen is still challenging due to the natural occurrence of oxygen in the upper atmospheres of terrestrial planets.

A significant challenge in training machine learning models on large-scale, geographically dispersed data is the slow speed of communication between devices. To address this issue, we propose a novel random walk approach that models the data distribution and its dynamics using a matrix-based method. This technique effectively eliminates the need for devices to exchange information with each other, as they only update their local knowledge based on interactions with neighboring devices. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a real-world image classification task.

A study conducted in 2019 by the Italian National Institute of Statistics in Lombardy, Italy, analyzed the impact of mental health treatment on the reoffending rates of individuals convicted of violent crimes, property crimes, and personal injuries. By examining administrative data from various Italian regions in northern Italy, researchers linked hospitalization records with criminal data for over 100,000 individuals convicted of violent crimes, property crimes, and personal injuries. The study found that mental health treatment significantly reduced the likelihood of reoffending, with a 13% decrease in the probability of committing another violent crime, a 10% reduction in property crimes, and a 14% reduction in personal injuries. The reduction in reoffending was primarily attributed to a decrease in repeat offenses of the same type, rather than switching to different kinds of crimes. The study also discovered that the reduction in reoffending was more pronounced for those convicted of less severe crimes, as well as for individuals who committed crimes against strangers.

A key challenge in medical image segmentation is the limited availability of annotated images. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages unannotated images through a new interpolation-based mixing strategy. This strategy creates images with unannotated boundaries by linearly combining the images' edges, and then uses these modified images to refine the model's predictions in the mid-range of the image. Our approach has been evaluated on three image datasets, and the results show that it outperforms current state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods.

Using graph neural networks (GNNs), we can efficiently analyze the local atomic arrangements in materials. However, the underlying models lack interpretability, hindering our ability to understand their behavior. To address this issue, we developed a new model called Local Environment Decomposition GNN (LED-GNN), which breaks down the high-dimensional input data into discrete graph elements, including node and edge features. By leveraging set-based attention mechanisms, LED-GNN learns the significance of each feature and explores their relationships. We demonstrate that this approach significantly enhances the model's performance on various tasks, including property prediction and molecular generation, while also providing a clear, localized explanation for each data point. Furthermore, our model outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in multiple benchmark scenarios, and the proposed local explanation can be validated by both human experts and generative agents.

If a function of a parameter $\theta$ in a statistical model is estimated through the method of moments, the estimation of this parameter can be viewed as weak convergence in the space of functions of another parameter $\pi$. This paper investigates the estimation of functions of parameters when the statistical model is parametric and estimates are obtained through the method of moments. Specifically, it derives the asymptotic behavior of the estimators in terms of their distribution under a measure that is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. This analysis is then applied to obtain the asymptotic distribution of the inverse of the parameter, as well as the estimation of functions of $\pi$ and the estimation of the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

Deep learning approaches to knowledge tracing have seen significant advancements, but their evaluation remains a challenge due to the lack of reliable and scalable human-generated datasets. To address this issue, we have developed a large-scale human-generated dataset called KTracer, which consists of 10,000 summaries of student knowledge states based on their task performance. Our KTracer dataset is designed to be scalable, allowing for the easy creation of new data entries. We have also conducted experiments to validate the effectiveness of KTracer, showing that it outperforms existing public datasets. Our research highlights the critical need for high-quality, reliable, and scalable human-generated datasets to support the development of educational assessment tools.

Elliptic operators in physics often exhibit elliptic behavior, which can be described as having a right inverse. This concept is well-established in $\mathbb{R}^n$ but becomes more complex in curved spaces. A curved space is defined by a smooth manifold, and the difficulty of finding a curved space that allows for the resolution of a specific type of elliptic operator is known as the obstruction problem. In this context, we investigate the relationship between the properties of a curved space and the types of elliptic operators that can be defined on it. Specifically, we define a new property called curved-space surjectivity, which extends the concept of surjectivity to include curved spaces. We then define a new class of elliptic operators, which we call curved-space elliptic operators, and investigate their properties. In particular, we show that the relationship between curved-space surjectivity and curved-space ellipticity is not symmetric, which means that the types of operators that can be defined on a curved space is not necessarily the same in both directions. In this investigation, we also examine the connection between curved-space surjectivity and the cohomology of the manifold, which provides additional insight into the relationship between curved spaces and elliptic operators.

In response to a request from the PxTP workshop, we have updated the veriT proof format to address the concerns raised during the discussions. These modifications have been incorporated into version 2020-10-27 of the veriT SAT solver.

In the realm of large-scale machine learning, distributed training is essential, yet it poses significant data privacy risks. A promising solution lies in federated learning, which allows multiple parties to collaborate on a shared model without exchanging their data. However, federated learning struggles to scale effectively with an increasing number of participants. We introduce FedBuff, an innovative approach that enables each node to contribute to a smaller, more manageable model by training a personal copy locally, periodically syncing it with the main model on a central server. This allows nodes with limited data to train locally and exchange it with others, while those with ample data can focus on the larger model. Our method ensures that the collaborative process maintains data privacy and achieves the same efficiency as traditional distributed training, even in terms of computational complexity. Experiments on diverse datasets and models demonstrate FedBuff's ability to scale model size and the number of participating nodes without sacrificing model performance or training speed, while upholding data privacy.

Recent advancements in automatic speech recognition using deep learning have led to significant improvements in performance. Transfer learning, a technique where a model trained on one task is adapted for a related task, has also been applied to enhance speech recognition. However, there is still uncertainty about how transfer learning affects speech recognition across different languages, especially when dealing with languages that are not closely related. This study evaluates the effectiveness of using BERT-based pretrained models for improving speech recognition across different languages. The results show that transfer learning can lead to performance gains when the target language has less similarity to the source language, but in other cases, fine-tuning with the target language data yields better results. Notably, incorporating a small amount of labeled data from the target task significantly enhances the transfer learning approach. Furthermore, this study finds that models trained on textual data are more effective than those trained on speech data for the purpose of transfer learning.

Underwater navigation tasks are notoriously time-consuming to optimize using conventional reinforcement learning methods. To address this issue, we propose a novel policy evaluation algorithm called SPGP-SARSA, which leverages sparse Gaussian process SARSA. This algorithm significantly reduces the number of samples required for policy evaluation by identifying and evaluating the most informative states, thereby improving efficiency. We incorporate a new state selection method that utilizes an acquisition function to identify the most valuable states to evaluate, and we update both the value function and policy accordingly. We also introduce a simple yet effective way to handle continuous state and action spaces. The SPGP-SARSA algorithm's performance is demonstrated through simulation experiments, which show that it reduces evaluation time while maintaining comparable policy optimization performance to conventional methods.

To find solutions to a system of differential equations describing a static, spherically symmetric, relativistic stellar model composed of two fluid components with different pressures and densities, we can derive the solutions from a single-fluid model with one fluid dependent on the other. This approach allows us to identify solutions where the relationship between the two fluids is linear, leading to a single equation and a reduced number of variables. By utilizing this method, we can obtain solutions to the two-fluid system for four known single-fluid solutions, including those by H. A. Buchdahl, I. Horvath and A. Perjes, and N. S. Landau and E. Lifshits, which previously required two-fluid derivations.

We investigate the challenge of adapting a general-purpose language model to specific tasks using scarce task-specific data, by framing it as a multi-task transfer learning problem. We apply this approach to natural language processing tasks with limited annotated data, such as grammar error correction and spelling correction. We find that using the same model architecture for different tasks can lead to negative transfer effects. To address this, we propose a novel GEC adaptation method that leverages the strengths of one-task learning and another with scarce data, by selectively combining gradients. We demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms traditional transfer learning methods on multiple datasets, including the CoNLL 2014 GEC dataset and the CSDCorpus Chinese GEC dataset. Our results show that our method achieves an F1-score of 86.2 on the CoNLL 2014 GEC dataset and an improvement of 2.4 points over the baseline on the CSDCorpus Chinese GEC dataset.

We introduce two novel fair division mechanisms for dividing a divisible good among self-interested agents with arbitrary valuations. The first mechanism, Round-Robin, involves agents sequentially choosing small segments of the good in a predetermined order, resulting in an allocation that satisfies envy-freeness up to any small segment. The second mechanism, Cut-and-Choose-$n$, has one agent dividing the good into $n$ segments, after which all agents choose a segment, guaranteeing an outcome that is envy-free up to any small segment for at least one agent. Both mechanisms require minimal information about the agents' valuations. We prove that, for any given valuation profile, there exists a segment allocation that meets the envy-free up to any small segment criterion for at least one agent, and similarly, a round in which a segment is chosen that fulfills this criterion for at least one agent. We establish that the utility obtained by any agent using Round-Robin is at least as high as what they would have obtained using Cut-and-Choose-$n$, and that these mechanisms are strategy-proof. We also demonstrate that Round-Robin and Cut-and-Choose-$n$ cannot be improved upon in terms of social welfare, and that they are optimal in minimizing the number of valuations required. We further show that no deterministic mechanism can guarantee an outcome that is Pareto efficient for at least one agent, and that any mechanism that ensures an envy-free up to any small segment outcome for at least one agent

U.S. 8839, a low inclination spiral galaxy located 13.5 megaparsecs away, has been studied to understand its structure and composition. We used deep imaging to map its stars and used this to determine the distances to different parts of the galaxy. Spectroscopic analysis of its hydrogen regions helped us locate them precisely and assess their chemical makeup. We found that these regions are spread across the galaxy's radius, with a significant concentration in the outer parts. Comparing U.S. 8839 to other similar galaxies revealed that its structure and star formation patterns are quite similar. Its gas distribution and star formation rate were also found to be in line with predictions from previous studies.

Using state-of-the-art lattice QCD calculations, we have conducted a comprehensive study of the lightest scalar ($\sigma$) and pseudoscalar ($\pi$) meson nonet, focusing on their properties across a wide range of quark masses. By employing a 2+1-flavour MILC gauge configuration ensemble and applying a covariantariant partial quenching technique to explore beyond physical quark masses, we have calculated the masses and decay constants of the nonet's ground state. Notably, we have determined the quark content of the $\pi$ and $\sigma$ mesons through the calculation of their scalar and pseudoscalar form factors, as well as their corresponding charges. Furthermore, we have examined the impact of varying quark masses on these quantities. The results obtained from this research provide valuable insights into the behavior of the lightest scalar and pseudoscalar meson nonet under different lattice QCD conditions.

We examined the T Cha classical T Tauri star, revealing extreme variability in its accretion rate over a 100-day period, varying by more than an order of magnitude. This variability is irregular and unpredictable, with significant changes occurring within just a few days. Our findings challenge the widely accepted view of steady disk evolution in T Cha, as evidenced by inconsistent interpretations of previous observational data. We propose that T Cha's variability may be linked to magnetic reconnection events occurring within a multi-scale accretion structure. The observed properties of T Cha's accretion rate variability provide a framework for future studies of similar stars.

SIT, or Shared Individual Trajectories, is a novel framework for offline multi-agent reinforcement learning. In this approach, individual agents process their own trajectories as well as those of other agents in the environment, and a separate model is trained for each agent to predict future states based on shared representations of the trajectories. This enables the system to generalize to previously unseen states and actions. SIT provides significant performance improvements over existing methods, achieving a 10% to 50% reduction in expected steps to reach a goal in offline reinforcement learning tasks, and also demonstrating successful application to high-dimensional continuous state spaces.

This paper introduces a novel network architecture for medical image registration, utilizing convolutional neural networks to estimate deformation fields directly from paired images. To address the high-dimensional input and output spaces, as well as the local nature of convolutional operations, we incorporate multiple components into our framework, including inverse convolutions, sparse sampling layers, and several subnetworks designed to model local and global deformations. Experimental results on 2D and 32D datasets demonstrate that our network achieves highly accurate image registration, outperforming traditional intensity-based methods by a significant margin, with performance improvements of over 0.5dB in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, our network is capable of producing accurate registrations for images with up to 20cm mismatches, making it a valuable tool for a range of medical applications, including image mosaicing, motion compensation, and data augmentation.

We investigate single-particle entanglement in a solid-state system consisting of a lattice with a single type of mobile particle. Due to the conservation of the particle number, single-particle entanglement cannot be the sole cause of nonlocal quantum effects and cannot be used to explain nonlocal behavior or facilitate a quantum advantage in communication scenarios. Nonetheless, single-particle entanglement can lead to nonlocal mean-field effects and facilitates a form of local-to-nonlocal mapping in certain cases.

This paper introduces a novel security and privacy preservation framework for vehicle communication systems based on blockchain and secure multiparty computation.
In this framework, roadside units are divided into trusted and untrusted categories, and roadside units collaborate to compute and share traffic data securely.
To prevent data tampering, the blockchain stores the hash values of traffic data, and the consensus mechanism is bypassed for data storage due to its high computational cost.
The proposed scheme leverages the batch secret reconstruction property of the polynomial secret sharing scheme to enhance data security and efficiency.
Theoretical analysis and simulation results demonstrate the improved security and performance of this new approach.

Observations of V392 Persei were conducted using the 1.2-meter telescope at SAASTO between April 1999 and January 2000, following its nova eruption in April 1999. The observations covered the visual spectrum and included the measurement of the absolute magnitude, which was found to be $M_V = -10.4 \pm 0.2$ at its peak brightness. The light curve exhibited a plateau phase lasting approximately 100 days, which was 10 times longer than that of typical IKN novae. The ejecta density of V392 Persei was estimated to be 10 times greater than the solar value, which was inferred from the absorption lines in the spectra. The spectra also showed a significant amount of neutral hydrogen, which was 100 times greater than that of typical IKN novae. In multi-user massive MIMO systems, pilot contamination and limited pilot resources pose significant challenges. This paper proposes a feedback-based encoding scheme to mitigate pilot contamination and enable unique pilot sequences for all users, even when the number of antennas is significantly lower than the total number of users. In this approach, each user is assigned a unique low-dimensional code, which is a feedback of its own location, and transmits this code instead of a unique pilot sequence. The base station then clusters users based on their feedback, estimates channels using short unique pilots, and refines pilot sequences. Feedback encoding is demonstrated to provide a feedback-based encoding scheme that offers a unique pilot sequence with a shorter estimation time and lower overhead compared to traditional Lloyd clustering methods. Simulation results show that the proposed scheme outperforms traditional pilot sequences in terms of MSE and sum rate, particularly in scenarios with a large number of users and antennas.

We demonstrate that a two-dimensional system's surface current model maintains its integrity under strong disorder, even when the system reaches the delocalized state. This model is easily driven and can be manipulated to transition between bosons and fermions. We examine its behavior in the presence of varying levels of disorder in the model's parameters. Notably, the surface current persists with moderate disorder in the bulk, but ceases to exist in the two cases of extreme delocalization. Reaching these extreme conditions requires a complex process, allowing us to precisely pinpoint the delocalized state's onset and observe how it responds to fermionic or bosonic behavior. Furthermore, we can drive the model out of equilibrium and find that surface currents persist, but with reduced stability.

We investigate Brans-Dicke theory, specifically focusing on a massless scalar field in the context of general relativity's branching theory. Our study involves analyzing the Brans-Dicke wave equation under the influence of a massless scalar field. We examine two main scenarios: a static star and a rotating black hole emitting a burst of radiation. In the case of a static star, we determine the conditions under which photons can escape to infinity, contingent upon the Brans-Dicke radiation diminishing to zero. In the case of a rotating black hole, we identify the conditions under which the black hole emits a burst of radiation and subsequently decays into a standard Schwarzschild solution.

This study examines the joint optimization of secure transmission precoders and power allocation in an integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) system, where multiple base station antennas transmit data to users and radar signals to various targets, while being vulnerable to an eavesdropper intercepting the transmitted signal. To address this issue, we formulate a non-convex minimax problem that takes into account the impact of power allocation at the base station and the satellite on system security. To solve this challenge, we develop an iterative algorithm that allocates power at different nodes in the network, revealing the base of the station as the most effective node for enhancing system security. To solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem, we employ the successive convex approximation (SCA) method. Numerical results demonstrate the base of the station as the optimal node for power allocation, and the radar node's power allocation has a limited impact on system security.

The creation of simulated environments for natural language manipulation tasks has been gaining traction recently. However, the high computational costs associated with large-scale experiments hinder their widespread adoption. We present TextWorldExpress, a set of simulated environments that have been significantly optimized for speed, achieving a 100-fold increase in processing rates compared to the original versions. This advancement enables researchers to conduct more extensive and computationally intensive studies in the field of language processing.

Deep learning models have achieved significant success in various fields, including image recognition and natural language processing. However, their widespread adoption is hindered by the substantial computational resources and energy consumption required for training and inference. To overcome this challenge, this paper presents a novel hardware architecture, the FDHT-LSTM, which combines a tensor-decomposed model with a specific inference model, FDHT, enabling efficient inference of recurrent neural networks. The FDHT-LSTM architecture decomposes data into manageable tensors, allowing for parallel processing and increased efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate the FDHT-LSTM's superiority over existing hardware, with a 1.8x to 10.6x improvement in inference speed and a 1.4x to 6.8x enhancement in energy consumption for common RNN tasks.

In spaces with anti-de Sitter geometry, the principles of the Weak Gravity Conjecture are intricately linked to various concepts, including the difficulty of negative cosmological constant values, the difficulty of local quantum field theories, and the notion of "self-binding energy" in quantum field theories. When formulating the WGC in AdS spaces, it is necessary to take into consideration the upper bound of the possible values of the cosmological constant. This study focuses on establishing the WGC in AdS spaces by demonstrating that sufficiently heavy states with unconfined charges exist, which can overcome the barriers of being bound to a particle and overrunning the critical point where anti-de Sitter space ceases to exist. This approach is particularly useful in understanding how the WGC in AdS spaces can be achieved in scalar field theories with self-binding energies exceeding mass thresholds and with the cosmological constant becoming positive.

This study examines the all-or-none order design in Germany's redisdispatch markets and its impact on grid operator procurement. Given a convex cost function, we demonstrate that the all-or-none design yields the same results as other designs when there is a single consumer, but can lead to higher procurement costs in certain instances when there are multiple consumers. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of consumer valuation distribution on the all-or-none design's tendency to maximize procurement costs in scenarios with multiple consumers. Our findings indicate that as the distribution of consumer valuations becomes more dispersed, the design's impact becomes more pronounced. To mitigate the design's negative effects, we propose a randomized all-or-none design that guarantees no worse outcomes than the standard design in any given scenario.

Given a field $K$ with a non-trivial valuation, we examine the Galois group $\Gamma$ of a generic separable quartic equation in $K$ whose coefficients are not constant. It has been established that for parabolic Galois groups, specifically those in $V_A$, the set of Galois groups equivalent to $\Gamma$ forms a negligible subset within the collection of all possible Galois groups, denoted as $\mathrm{Gal}(4,K)$. In contrast, for the remaining, hyperbolic set of Galois groups, known as $V_D$, the locus of $\Gamma$ forms a substantial subset within the collection of possible Galois groups, meaning there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that the set of Galois groups containing $\Gamma$ has a density of at least $c$ within $\mathrm{Gal}(4,K)$. This outcome extends to the case where the field $K$ is the field of polynomials over a finite field, thereby providing support for the conjecture proposed by Poonen and Rubinstein regarding the proportion of extensions that yield a specific Galois group, namely $S_4$. Furthermore, the Polynomials Analogue of the Bateman-Horn Conjecture can be rephrased in terms of the distribution of Galois groups, enabling us to demonstrate that this conjecture is not universally valid, given its failure to hold for certain sets defined by specific conditions.

Saturn's polar stratosphere has been extensively studied since the entry of the Saturn probe into its final orbit in 2019.  The stratospheric temperatures at Saturn's north pole have been well-documented, revealing a cold vortex in the summer and a warm spiral in the winter.  In contrast, the dynamics of Saturn's south pole have been less understood due to limited observational data.  The south pole's summer vortex has been characterized as an exceptionally cold feature, with temperatures as low as 90 K near the pole, which is significantly colder than the equatorial average.  The presence of a persistent cold polar cap has been confirmed, with the south pole's average temperature being 5-10 K colder than the equator.  The discovery of a standing planetary wave in the south pole's summer stratosphere has been made, with the wave's behavior being comparable to that observed at Jupiter's north pole.  The south pole's winter has been found to be warmer than the equator, with the presence of a cold vortex being uncertain.  The discovery of a cold polar stratospheric vortex in the south pole's autumn has been made, with the feature being comparable to the cold polar stratospheric vortex observed at the north pole.  The vortex has been found to be exceptionally cold, with temperatures as low as 70 K near the pole, and with the polar stratosphere being 20 K colder than the equator.

In this study, we examine the positive solution to the Schrödinger equation in a confined domain with a non-zero source term that behaves like $1/|x|^2$ near the origin. Unlike previous research, we consider a situation where the boundary of the domain does not match the domain itself. By utilizing a combination of variational methods and a technique called Pohozaev's identity, we successfully demonstrate the blow-up of the solution under certain conditions. Moreover, we further analyze the behavior of a sequence of functions that lead to a concentrated blow-up at a specific point on the domain, resulting in a precise description of how the sequence behaves as it approaches infinity.

To effectively leverage the vast array of established results in commutative algebra, a key strategy is to transform problems from characteristic-zero to those in characteristic greater than zero. A novel approach is introduced to address the limitations of existing automated reasoning tools that are restricted to positive characteristic, by utilizing a framework known as differential algebra. This approach involves reinterpreting variables in a characteristic-greater-than-zero setting as differential operators in characteristic-zero, thereby enabling the use of highly efficient automated reasoning tools. This technique has already been successfully applied to prove the absolute irreducibility of the Jacobian of the KdS equation's family of semi-simple solutions, for the first time, in an entirely automated manner.

This text discusses the symplectical double vector bundle as an extension of symmetric double vector bundles, which have an established correspondence with Lagrangian double vector bundles and serve as symplectical structures on tangent double vector bundles. The concept is further explored in higher dimensions, where the symplectical (n,c)-fold vector bundles are defined in terms of their folding properties and tangent (n,c)-fold vector bundles are described in relation to their symplectical structures.

Geometric structures, including various versions of Kirillov's measure, are naturally arising from the intrinsic properties of Lie algebras. This approach, while insightful, lacks rigorous justification. This paper aims to rectify that deficiency by deriving relations between geometric measures in different settings, including the case of real reductive groups, where we establish a direct proportionality between measures in the geometric framework and those of Riemannian structure, under the assumption of an absolutely flat norm, which is not typical.

To reconstruct energy spectra in x-ray scattering experiments, particularly at the x-ray ring facilities, phase retrieval algorithms are commonly utilized.  
However, existing methods are either computationally intensive or lack robustness in handling high-energy ranges.  
A novel phase algorithm is presented that overcomes these limitations by employing a maximum likelihood estimation approach, which enables accurate energy reconstruction across the entire x-ray energy range with a minimal computational requirement.  
This new algorithm is successfully applied to reconstruct energy spectra from x-ray polarimetry data, yielding a precise polarimetry measurement.

This method models the interaction between blocked and open fractures. A variable transformation has been used to reformulate the model into a real-valued system of equations. A system of equations consisting of two equations was then derived to describe the behavior of the transformation variable. A two-parameter family of functions called Dirac-$\beta$ has been introduced as a way to handle the singularities in the reformulated system. A function called Dirac-$\beta$ has been shown to approach a real-valued system of equations in a specific limit. A function called Dirac-$\beta$ has been shown to satisfy a system of equations consisting of two equations. A two-parameter family of functions has been used to construct a closed system of equations. A family of functions has been constructed to satisfy the closed system of equations. A family of functions has been constructed to handle the blocking of fractures in porous media.

In the field of machine learning, selecting a subset of hypotheses from a large set that optimizes performance is a key challenge. Decision-making in hypothesis selection typically involves evaluating outcomes under different conditions, but this process is complicated by the difficulty of accurately modeling utility functions. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that represents utility functions using a linear combination of coefficients and feature values, allowing for the efficient estimation of model parameters through optimization techniques. This method enables the use of both continuous and discrete features, and can be applied to both structured and unstructured data. Furthermore, our approach allows for the incorporation of non-linear features and can be used to select a subset of hypotheses that maximizes performance, even in large-scale datasets.

In 2018, we introduced DiscSense, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 10,000 annotated connections between discourse markers and their underlying semantic relationships. To fill a significant gap in current research, we provided the community with an updated version of DiscSense, featuring improved discourse marker labels and a wider variety of annotated semantic relationships. We also explored the development of a sentiment analysis system tailored for discourse markers, comparing two approaches: a basic classifier that predicts overall sentence sentiment and an advanced one that incorporates discourse relations. The results of this investigation were presented and discussed in detail.

We examine geodesic strong convexity and smoothness properties on a specific manifold of factored matrices for objectives in matrix optimization of the form $f(X)=f(XX^{\top})$. Assuming the original objective $f(X)$ exhibits restricted strong convexity and smoothness with certain parameters, we demonstrate that the factorized objective $f(XX^{\top})$ also exhibits geodesic strong convexity and smoothness with corresponding parameters that depend on those of the original objective and the dimensions of the input and output spaces. This analysis leads to improved convergence rate guarantees for first-order methods on the manifold of factored matrices, as well as convergence rate guarantees for methods that are not geodesic.

A strong edge-coloring of a graph with a maximum degree of $d$ in a bipartite setting involves coloring its edges in $s \geq d^2$ colors such that any three edges forming a triangle have three distinct colors. In 1990, A. Jaeger proposed a conjecture that all 3-regular graphs can be strongly edge-colored using just 9 colors. In 2015, this conjecture was disproven by B. Brešar et al. who found a counterexample with 21 colors. We further found a counterexample to this conjecture by exhibiting an infinite family of bipartite graphs that cannot be strongly edge-colored with 9 colors. We also found that for any star-free bipartite graph with a maximum degree of 3, it is possible to strongly edge-color it using 10 colors.

This study employs a co-evolutionary genetic algorithm to explore the effectiveness of a distance-based modification to a basic Hamming distance metric in a best-response dynamics framework. The primary objective is to lower the average distance from the Nash Equilibrium state in a dataset comprising 100 synthetic binary classification problems. The results indicate that incorporating information about the genetic population can lead to outcomes of lower quality than standard approaches. Furthermore, when comparing basic and population-informed distance metrics in their impact on expected hamming distance from Nash Equilibrium, the basic metric produces more favorable results. The study also compares the effects of these metrics on population and reproductive strategies.

Consider a weighted oriented graph $\mathcal{F}$ within a class of weighted oriented trees and cycles, and show that the edge ideal $I(\mathcal{F})$ has an property where its ordinary symbolic power equals its regular one for a specific power value. In contrast, we provide an example within this class where a higher symbolic power exceeds a regular one. In addition, we establish that the set of integer values where the equality holds is not necessarily connected.

Various techniques, including non-uniform weight reduction, have been proposed to prevent silent data corruptions in web-based neural network applications. These methods typically limit the magnitude of individual network weights within specific thresholds. However, current approaches are susceptible to false positives, leading to the rejection of legitimate data corruptions and potentially leaving critical security vulnerabilities undetected. We address this issue by proposing novel non-uniform range restriction methods that leverage statistical information from network traffic to dynamically determine the magnitude limits for individual bytes. Our approach, known as NURR, has been demonstrated through experiments on real-world traffic data to significantly reduce false positives and enhance the reliability of silent data corruption detection. Our findings indicate that the initial methods based on uniform weight reduction detection are prone to false positives, accounting for up to 40% of rejected alerts in some cases.

We investigate the Jordanian twist implementation within the classical Yangians of the adjoint $gl(N)$ algebra under the adjoint elliptic Drinfel'd-Sokolov twist, for all adjoint elliptic Adler-Kostant-Symes systems of differential equations. Through the application of the Jordanian twist, we establish a direct connection between Yang-Elliptic and Adj Yang-Elliptic conserved quantities. Furthermore, we derive the modified far-adjoint Yang-Elliptic conserved quantities via the Jordanian twist from the modified far-adjoint Yang-Elliptic conserved quantities obtained through the Adler-Kostant-Symes twist. Notably, we prove the universal validity of this approach for all orders of expansion in the adjoint elliptic Drinfel'd-Sokolov and Adler-Kostant-Symes variables, under the assumption of sufficient non-degeneracy in these variables. In the case of the degenerate case, we recover the results previously obtained for the $sl(N)$ adjoint $gl(N)$ Yang-Elliptic conserved quantities.

This paper presents a new approach for the task of name tagging in languages with limited resources, which combines the use of parallel sentences and entity names. We've developed a novel method that incorporates entity names into a neural network based name tagger using an attention mechanism, which allows the model to selectively focus on relevant parts of the entity name for each label. Our approach is evaluated on four languages, and the results show a significant improvement in performance compared to using parallel sentences alone. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate that adding entity names leads to better performance than using neural machine translation to convert names to their target language form.

In this study, measurements of various particle ratios, including kaons, pions, and protons, were conducted for BGO fragments of larger datasets comprising 3.04 fb$^{-1}$ of pp data at $\sqrt{s} = 8$ TeV and 139 nb$^{-1}$ of PbPb data at $\sqrt{s} = 5.02$ TeV. Notably, the observed particle ratios align with previous LHC findings and follow a consistent pattern across both small and large collision events as they transition from 8 to 5.02 TeV to 13 TeV. Furthermore, the PbPb data exhibits significant flow effects, which can be effectively replicated using a percolation model.

The intricate relationship between a city's infrastructure layout and the patterns of civil disturbances has long fascinated urban sociologists and geographers.  In this study, we investigate the impact of a city's infrastructure topology on the dynamics of civil unrest using a modified version of the Ising model.  By applying this model to both regular and random regular graphs that represent the topology of a city's infrastructure, we simulate the spread of unrest and observe its patterns over time.  Our results reveal that the topology of a city's infrastructure significantly influences the dynamics of civil unrest, with the model exhibiting a phase transition in its behavior.  Specifically, we find that the model exhibits two distinct phases: a period of rapid unrest propagation followed by a period of slow decay.  In the case of random regular graphs, we observe that the model's topological properties lead to a period of exponential growth in the number of affected nodes, followed by a period of polynomial decay.  In contrast, the model's behavior on regular graphs exhibits a different pattern of propagation and decay.  In summary, our study provides new insights into the relationship between a city's infrastructure topology and the dynamics of civil unrest, with implications for the design of urban infrastructure and the management of civil disturbances.

This research presents a novel and efficient symbolic method for assessing when the preimage of a regular expression is contained within another regular expression, based on the characteristics of a system of dynamical variables. This method is innovative in its use of Brzozowski's operator to regular expressions, which allows for the application of a fundamental theorem from control theory, specifically the Bertinucci-Sontag theorem. This application enables the determination of containment by checking the equivalence of expressions, a process that can be accomplished using existing algorithms. We provide an alternative, potentially more efficient way to check containment by leveraging the power series expansion of expressions and applying the Gol'den'shtein-Rey theorem. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by checking the preimage containment for linear fractional systems, a result that had been previously established by other researchers. We also present an alternative, more efficient way to check the linear fractional system preimage containment by leveraging the power series expansion of expressions and applying the Gol'den'shtein-Rey theorem.

Traditional Visual Inertial Odometry (VIO) algorithms extract explicit features from input images, which are then used to estimate motion. In contrast, deep learning-based VIO models directly process raw image data, bypassing the need for feature extraction. These models have shown significant improvements in performance, particularly in complex and dynamic environments. However, they often suffer from limited generalizability when applied to new scenarios. This paper presents a novel deep learning-based VIO model that generalizes effectively across various environments by leveraging self-supervised learning. The model achieves this generalizability through the use of a lightweight descriptor network, which enables it to capture the correspondence of visual landmarks. This network is trained using a descriptor matching loss, which is optimized by employing a global motion estimator based on the Wide and Efficient Visual Odometry (WEO) model. The descriptor matching loss is further enhanced with an epipolar geometric constraint. To train the network in a self-supervised manner, an image re-synthesis network is employed to reconstruct images based on estimated camera poses and matched descriptors. The proposed model has been successfully applied to diverse datasets, including those with monocular and multi-sensor configurations. Experimental results demonstrate the model's superior generalizability compared to traditional VIO algorithms and other deep learning-based methods.

We present a theoretical framework for three-dimensional three-leg Hombic lattices, which incorporates both two-dimensional and three-dimensional chiral-charge patterns, and suggests a path towards understanding "topological Hall effects" in three-dimensional higher-order Weyl semimetals. By applying a tight-binding model to this lattice, we identify three distinct phases: one with two-dimensional edge states, another with a network of four Weyl points in momentum space, and a third where the Weyl points are situated on different high-symmetry lines, necessitating different mathematical approaches to extract their topological characteristics. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate how these topological properties manifest in real space, specifically in terms of electric and magnetic responses, and we visualize their effects through various currents in response to external electric and magnetic fields. Furthermore, by applying a perturbation to the model, we show that the complex topological structure can be simplified, resulting in a phase characterized by three Weyl points lying on the same high-symmetry line, and we investigate its topological characteristics and associated surface and bulk states.

A key challenge in image and video restoration is data completion, particularly in scenarios where missing data is significant. This paper presents a novel numerical method for tackling this issue, focusing on a specific application: reconstructing a diverging gravitational wave signal from incomplete interferometric data. We employ edge finite elements to accurately capture the parabolic pattern in the data and achieve precise results even with a limited number of degrees of freedom. This approach also ensures stable and reliable performance when dealing with incomplete datasets of varying sizes. Our method achieves second-order convergence rates and can be effectively solved using iterative solvers with local preconditioning techniques.

We propose a novel knowledge amalgamation approach for training knowledge graphs, which amalgamates external knowledge bases with existing graph data. Our approach amalgamates knowledge by leveraging a saliency-based method to determine the most valuable pieces of external knowledge for the target task. We begin by training a student model using only the existing graph data, then identify the most informative external knowledge fragments to aid in learning. Our model learns by amalgamating knowledge from the graph and the external data bases, using the previously identified external knowledge fragments. Our model demonstrates superior performance in multiple knowledge amalgamation scenarios, including language translation, entity resolution, and entity linking, outperforming state-of-the-art models that use both labeled and unlabeled data. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyangzhang/KGA.

Quantum quenches in spin systems are simulated using cold atoms, and measuring the resulting thermal states is a pressing issue. We establish a direct correlation between the irreversible entropy generated during a quantum quench and the temperature at which a quench that produces the same change in entropy is thermalized, and thus can be measured. We demonstrate this approach by simulating two distinct models, and we also examine the relationship between the generated entropy and the fidelity of the temperature determination.

We explore non-unitary dynamics in a quantum system interacting with its environment, considering the environment as an uncontrolled, complex, and vast component of the overall universe. By applying the concept of non-equilibrium non-unitary dynamics, we analyze the system's evolution, which exhibits time-reversal symmetry at both micro and macro levels. We demonstrate that the system's non-unitary evolution, when viewed through the lens of its environment, involves a coherent time-reversal process. This process, which we term time-twirling, is shown to be mathematically equivalent to a time-averaging process. Furthermore, we establish a connection between time-twirling and the time required to distinguish between two quantum states, which we term the non-unitary distinguishability time. This time, which can be influenced by the environment's complexity, is shown to be the key factor in achieving the non-unitary decoherence of a quantum state. Furthermore, we establish that time-twirling can be understood as a process that, in the limit of an infinitely complex environment, leads to the complete loss of information about the system's initial state, rendering it indistinguishable from a maximally mixed state. This process, which we term the time-twirl, is shown to be a universal mechanism that, when combined with non-unitary dynamics, provides a rigorous explanation for the emergence of the Born rule in the context of quantum decoherence.

This paper proves the existence of a regular simplex with vertices in the unit cube $Q_n$, specifically a nondegenerate regular simplex of dimension $d$, where $d < n$, is possible if and only if the number of interpolation nodes is at least $\frac{(3d+1)(d+2)}{2}$. Additionally, an explicit formula for the side length of the largest regular simplex in $Q_n$ is derived, and the side length of the largest regular simplex in $n$-dimensional space is calculated for various values of $n$.

The concept of planetology involves comprehending how a planet's internal and external systems interact over time. While the concept of recycling applies to various aspects of the planet, including its atmosphere, surface, and interior, its impact on atmospheric evolution is often limited to brief periods. Over extended timescales, the cycling within a planet's interior has a significant influence on its atmosphere's development. To better understand the atmosphere of Venus, it is crucial to analyze its prolonged evolution in conjunction with the planet's interior dynamics. In this study, we have developed a coupled model that simulates the evolution of Venus's atmosphere and interior dynamics, including the planet's magnetic field, for a duration of 4 billion years. Utilizing this coupled model, we have explored the atmosphere's stability and its interaction with the planet's interior, including the production of iron, iron oxide, and the iron oxide photolysis cycle. By applying this model to Venus, we have gained valuable insights that can also be used to study the atmospheres of terrestrial exoplanets.

In multivariate point process models, particularly for their application in predicting time series, the nonlinear Hawkes process stands out due to its ability to capture complex interactions. To estimate this process accurately, it's crucial to account for certain characteristics that reflect the underlying data. This paper introduces a new method for parameter estimation that utilizes an optimization-based approach, incorporating a general class of nonlinear point processes. The study specifically investigates the nonlinear Hawkes process, providing explicit formulas for its statistical properties and developing a new statistical test to validate process linearity. Additionally, statistical inference methods for nonlinear parameters are explored, including maximum likelihood estimation and a Bayesian approach. The proposed methods are illustrated through numerical experiments and real-world data analysis of cryptocurrency prices.

A novel concept, a plasma waveplate, is proposed to correct linear polarisation in linear polarimetric imagers for polarisation-sensitive spectral cameras on satellites. The required thickness of the plate is influenced by the camera's spectral range, electron density, and plasma characteristics, which can be manipulated to achieve a specific quarter-wavelength condition at a target frequency. Despite the potential for a very thick plate, thinner alternatives can be realised through the use of dielectric structures or surface patterns, albeit with some limitations. A prototype plasma waveplate was developed and tested, featuring a quarter-wavelength thickness of 1.5 cm at 10 MHz, with possible applications in other areas of polarisation spectroscopy.

By incorporating CP-violating effects from scalar fields, this model allows for a significantly larger value of the d_\tau compared to the Standard Theory, as it is not limited by the GIM mechanism. However, achieving a tau EDM value that surpasses the sensitivity of the upcoming International Linear Collider (d_\tau \gtrsim 10^{-17} e\cdot cm) requires extremely large values of the trilinear coupling \lambda_3 \gtrsim 1, which is inconsistent with current experimental data. Conversely, a future collider with higher luminosity could detect a d_\tau \sim 10^{-18} e\cdot cm for \lambda_3 \sim 1, making it feasible to explore a substantial portion of the model's viable parameter space.

The rank metric is one such type, and it has gained significant interest recently. The study of these systems in relation to the Birkhoff–Vandermonde basis has been explored, revealing the error correction capabilities for two specific cases. The first case shows that for a specific ratio, the systems can only correct a limited number of types of controllability issues, whereas for other ratios, the systems can correct a broader range of problems. The findings of this study reveal the difference in difficulty between these two cases and provide insights into the relationship between the systems' properties and their error correction capabilities.

These blocks, which are invariant under coordinate transformations, are shown to have a consistent relationship with sets of holomorphic and anti-holomorphic geodesic operators. By leveraging this connection, we derive the precise form of OPE blocks for specific current pairs and explore their correlation patterns with primary fields. Notably, a pair of conserved currents in the CFT$_{2}$ system can be expressed as a pair of AdS$_{2}$ geodesic operators in the bulk, and we provide explicit formulas for their OPE block pairs in relation to geodesic operators in the AdS$_{2}$ geometry. Furthermore, we establish the consistency of our results with existing literature and outline potential extensions to include spinning geodesic operators and anti-holomorphic geodesic paths.

A new image type, resembling a cross, has been developed to assess the structural integrity of lobster-eye optics systems. This novel image type is created using a point X-ray source positioned behind a system composed of V-groove microchannel plates. By rotating the source through various angles, the distinct segments of the system can be identified and compared. Furthermore, analyzing the widths of the cross's arms provides valuable information about the characteristics of the X-ray source and the scattering properties of the system. By examining the widths of the cross's outer arms, the size of the X-ray source can be estimated, while the inner arms' widths offer insights into the system's scattering behavior.
